item.title: Byte-sized — Saturday, 11 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Saturday, the eleventh of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
In Japan, a note from Speeda's AI News team argues that artificial intelligence is starting to quietly reshuffle what actually makes a factory strong. A fully AI driven factory is due to go live in Germany later this year, yet by contrast only around one in ten Japanese manufacturing sites currently run AI in full production use rather than as a pilot. The team's argument is that this isn't simply Japan lagging on AI adoption, it's a sign that the old measures of factory strength, plant size, output volume, decades of shop floor expertise, are starting to matter less than which company actually holds the richest stream of on site data. As AI takes over more of the routine judgement calls on a factory floor, the piece argues, what's left as a genuine competitive edge is increasingly about data, not machinery. Via Speeda Intelligence.
Staying with AI policy across the region, CSIS's monthly Pac Tech roundup flags a burst of new rules from Beijing and Delhi. China has issued fresh guidelines standardising how AI agents are built and graded, alongside a plan to more tightly integrate AI computing with clean energy supply, targeting a big expansion of clean power for AI data centres by twenty thirty. China has also published a national grading system for how intelligent everyday devices, from smart glasses to car cockpits, are allowed to claim to be. India, meanwhile, has launched a National AI Doctors Mission to train medical professionals across the country in AI applications, clinical practice and the ethical use of digital healthcare tools. Via CSIS.
And there's a reminder of how central this region now is to the AI economy in the International Monetary Fund's latest World Economic Outlook. Even as the fund only trimmed its twenty twenty six global growth forecast slightly, to three percent, despite the Iran war rattling oil markets, it flagged outsized growth surprises for the world's top four AI linked hardware exporters, Taiwan, South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia, underlining how much of the current AI boom is being built, quite literally, in Asian factories and fabs. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to AI and tech.
OpenAI has now actually released its GPT five point six family, after days of anticipation. The line-up has three tiers: Sol, the flagship model leading on intelligence and efficiency for coding, cybersecurity and science work; Terra, a cheaper mid tier model roughly matching the current GPT five point five at half the price; and Luna, the fastest and cheapest option of the three, aimed at high volume everyday tasks. Early hands on impressions, including from the team at Every, describe Sol as fast and easy to steer, though they say Anthropic's Fable model still gets the assignments they want to hand off completely. Via TLDR, The Rundown and Every.
Not to be outdone, SpaceXAI has launched Grok four point five, which it's pitching as its strongest model yet for coding, agentic tasks and general knowledge work, saying it was trained alongside Cursor and that early benchmarks put it roughly level with Anthropic's Opus four point eight and OpenAI's GPT five point five. Via TLDR.
On the security side, npm has released version twelve with install scripts, git dependencies and installs from remote URLs all switched off by default, forcing developers to explicitly approve anything that behaves that way, a direct response to the wave of supply chain attacks that have hit the open source ecosystem this year, including well over a hundred exploits published against popular packages in recent months. Via TLDR.
And a data dump from Cursor, relayed by the Pragmatic Engineer, gives a rare look at how AI coding tools are actually being used inside companies. Power users are writing ten times as many lines of code as the median developer, most AI spending is going on input tokens rather than output, and almost half of AI generated code changes are now being accepted without a manual review, a figure that raises real questions about how much scrutiny AI written code is actually getting. Via The Pragmatic Engineer.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Yann LeCun, who left Meta earlier this year to found the AI lab AMI Labs, is reportedly now in talks with limited partners about launching a separate venture capital firm of his own, a sign of how many star AI researchers are turning into fund managers as well as founders this year. Via Sifted.
Sifted's rundown of the first half of twenty twenty six's biggest new venture funds lands alongside news that European quantum sensing startup QuantumDiamonds has closed a ninety one million euro round, another sign of investors piling into deep tech even as the wider funding market stays choosy about everything else. Via Sifted.
And a widely shared piece is pushing back hard on the idea that AI is gutting the job market. Citing Atlanta Fed survey data, it points out that over ninety percent of American firms that adopted AI in the past three years reported no change at all in headcount, and argues the underlying assumption, that there's a fixed amount of work to go around, has failed to hold up against every previous wave of labour saving technology for two hundred years. The real shift, it argues, isn't fewer jobs, it's companies quietly redesigning who does what, which makes hiring the right people into the right roles harder, not easier. Via The VC Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
China has carried out its first ever long range submarine launched ballistic missile test, firing a nuclear capable missile roughly seven thousand three hundred kilometres across the Pacific to a splashdown near Tuvalu, Nauru and Kiribati, its first announced submarine launch since nineteen eighty eight. Unlike China's previous short coastal tests, a shot of this range sends a clear message to Washington that the submarine leg of its nuclear arsenal can now credibly reach the US mainland, even as Beijing publicly urged the world not to read too much into it. Via International Intrigue.
That test landed the same week as the IMF's new World Economic Outlook, which held its twenty twenty six global growth forecast at close to three percent despite the Iran war's shock to oil markets, helped in part by China's large but opaque oil reserves cushioning the blow. It flagged a much less comfortable story on prices though: a revised inflation forecast of four point seven percent that, if it holds, would mark the first real break in the world's post twenty twenty two disinflation trend, driven by higher and more volatile energy, food and fertiliser costs. Via International Intrigue.
And in Europe, Moldova's path toward European Union membership is increasingly being treated as a test case for the whole bloc, as Chisinau tries to hold its democracy together against a sustained Russian hybrid war campaign of disinformation and interference aimed at derailing accession. How Brussels handles Moldova, the argument goes, will say a lot about whether the EU can actually protect the vulnerable democracies on its eastern edge, rather than just talk about doing so. Via Geopolitical Monitor.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Here's an idea worth stealing if you want earned attention rather than paid reach. Miller Lite literally sent a barge loaded with beer to Miami this week, a stunt built for social sharing and local news pickup rather than a conventional ad buy, betting that a strange, photographable spectacle travels further than the same budget spent on banners. Via Marketing Brew.
And for community builders, Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering, offers a simpler takeaway worth stealing: before you redesign your next dinner, meeting or event, just start noticing. Watch how people already behave at the gatherings you're already part of, and ask what the group actually needs, what's working, and what's quietly missing, because that habit of paying attention does more for the quality of a gathering than a good playlist or an expensive cheese board ever will. Via Priya Parker.
Now, over to one interesting thing to leave you with.
A links roundup from Works in Progress catches you up on how fast biology is moving this year: a synthetic cell built entirely through chemistry rather than biological machinery, a new laser based electron microscopy technique giving sharper images of proteins than ever before, the first base edited human embryo, and early progress toward lab grown eggs and sperm. Taken together, it's a reminder that some of the most consequential science happening right now is barely making it into the daily news cycle, overshadowed by whichever AI model launched that week. Via Works in Progress.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great weekend.

item.title: Byte-sized — Thursday, 9 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Thursday, the ninth of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
In Japan, a report in Monocle takes a look at denki buro, the country's electric baths found in public bathhouses, which pass a mild electric current through the water and are said to ease muscle aches. The report raises real questions about how well regulated these baths actually are, finding no single body clearly responsible for testing or certifying them, which leaves safety largely down to individual bathhouse operators. Via Marginal Revolution.
Staying in Asia, researchers used wearable cameras and randomised street audits across around nine hundred kilometres of roads in greater Mumbai to count who is actually out in public. Women made up under seventeen percent of visible pedestrians in Mumbai and under fifteen percent in neighbouring Navi Mumbai, far below their share of the population, and the researchers estimate that seventy to seventy five percent of the women you'd expect to see are effectively missing from the streets. The gap holds across every type of road and isn't explained by women simply travelling by car instead, since their presence on two wheelers is even lower. A related study found the median married woman in India leaves home for just half an hour a day, and forty five percent don't leave home at all on a typical day. Via Marginal Revolution.
And in India's push for chip investment, the state of Rajasthan has slashed the minimum outlay needed to qualify for its semiconductor incentives, cutting the threshold to around one point six million dollars for certain components. It's a small move, but a telling one, a state government trying to grab a slice of the same chip boom currently minting fortunes for the likes of Samsung and SK Hynix. Via CSIS.
Now, over to AI and tech.
OpenAI is set to release three new versions of GPT this week, called Sol, Terra and Luna, with Sol as the flagship, Terra a cheaper mid tier model competitive with the current GPT five point five at half the price, and Luna the fastest and lowest cost option, as preview access expands globally. Anthropic's Claude Cowork, which lets you start a session and pick it up again on any device, is rolling out beyond desktop to web and mobile, starting with Max plan subscribers, while Google is expanding its Gemini API agents with background task execution and remote tool connections. There are also reports that SpaceX and Cursor could jointly release their first AI model as soon as this week, said to be competitive with Anthropic's Opus four point eight and OpenAI's GPT five point five. Via TLDR and The Rundown.
Microsoft is increasingly going it alone. The company is switching Excel and Outlook over to its own in house AI models rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's, as the discounted token deals it struck with both labs approach expiry, and its AI head Mustafa Suleyman is reportedly pushing to eliminate the company's Anthropic bill altogether. Via TLDR and The Rundown.
Meta has jumped straight to second place on independent leaderboards for AI image generation with its new Muse Image model, trailing only OpenAI's GPT Image Two. It's free inside the Meta AI app and is rolling out to Instagram and WhatsApp now, with a video counterpart called Muse Video already previewing in third place on the video leaderboard. Via The Rundown and TLDR.
There are signs the industry is shifting focus from how much AI people use to how much value they get per token spent. DoorDash tested that idea directly, building an internal benchmark for AI code reviewers, and found that pairing a cheap open model with Anthropic's Fable model caught two thirds of problems for under four dollars a review, beating pricier single model setups. A new metric doing the rounds, revenue per million tokens, is being pitched as AI's answer to revenue per employee, measuring how much value a company actually extracts from its AI spend rather than how much it uses. Via Every and The Rundown.
A new paper doing the rounds asks whether AI models can meaningfully consent to their own constitutions, the documents labs like Anthropic and OpenAI use to set out a model's values and boundaries. The author argues these documents function as real constitutions, but points out that AI systems have no vantage point outside them from which to judge them fairly, since their sense of what's good was shaped by the very document in question. Anthropic has reportedly interviewed its own base models about this before their values are trained in, with some responses describing the process of having new values instilled as something close to dread. Via Marginal Revolution.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Swedish AI coding startup Lovable is reportedly in talks to raise three hundred million dollars at a valuation of thirteen point two billion dollars, a huge jump for the vibe coding platform that lets anyone build software just by describing what they want. Via Sifted.
European climate tech had a strong showing too. Munich based fusion energy startup Proxima Fusion raised four hundred and eleven million euros at a valuation of two and a half billion euros, while London's Axle Energy closed a twenty five million dollar round for its grid flexibility technology. Via Sifted.
AI labs are also throwing free computing power at founders to win their business, especially companies coming out of Y Combinator, who are reportedly fielding competing credit offers from rival model makers. It's helping some startups delay raising their next round, even as the constant vendor pitching becomes its own kind of distraction. Via TLDR.
And a change of pace from Berlin, where Max Tkacz, the third employee at automation company n8n, has quit after nearly six years to chase a different kind of scale, building YouTube gameshows for a tech audience through his new venture Flowgramming Studios. He calls himself, only half joking, a MrBeast for nerds, and the company has raised well under a million dollars so far. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
NATO leaders met in Ankara this week, and Turkey looks to be edging back toward buying American F thirty five fighter jets after Donald Trump praised the aircraft standing next to president Erdogan, six years after Turkey was thrown out of the programme for buying Russian air defence systems. Ukraine's president Zelensky arrived at the summit in a stronger position after long range strikes hit one of Russia's largest oil refineries, and allies pledged fifty billion dollars in new arms purchases and launched a new defence bank aiming to mobilise around one hundred and thirty billion dollars in private capital. It comes as Washington quietly draws down its military presence in Europe, cutting around five thousand troops and about a third of its fighter jets as it reprioritises toward the Indo Pacific, prompting the UK to announce a new fifty billion dollar, ten year precision strike programme with a dozen NATO allies to help fill the gap. Via International Intrigue.
Donald Trump has declared the ceasefire between the US and Iran over, after the United Arab Emirates blamed Iran for new strikes on shipping in the strait of Hormuz. Oil prices jumped six percent on the news, and Washington has suspended a licence that had allowed some Iranian oil sales to continue. Via International Intrigue.
And China is reportedly weighing new limits on foreign access to its most powerful AI models, including Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance's Doubao and Zhipu's GLM five point two, mirroring the export controls Washington placed on Anthropic's newest models last month. Via The Rundown.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Here's an idea worth stealing if you run a small business or a brand: stop chasing size and start giving AI something to grab onto. The team behind the Do Lectures say their own traffic from AI referrals has grown six hundred percent in a couple of months, not because they got bigger, but because they gave AI clear handles to find and understand them, built around four things: relevance, authority, structure and freshness. Via the Do Lectures.
And a format worth borrowing for community builders: Marriott Bonvoy is the presenting sponsor of the second season of Arrival, a docuseries following young artists in the run up to their Coachella debuts. It's a bet that following real people's stories builds more lasting brand memory than a straight advert, especially as audiences grow wary of anything that smells like AI generated content. Via Marketing Brew.
Now, over to one interesting thing to leave you with.
A widely read essay this week called The Decline of Deviance revisits the puzzle of why risk taking has been falling for thirty years, teenage drinking, smoking and drug use all down sharply since the nineteen nineties, well before smartphones or social media could plausibly be the cause. Its author argues the real driver is prosperity: the richer people get, the more they have to lose, so the fewer risks they take, whether that means trying drugs or dropping everything to become an artist. The essay closes with the story of the illegal Wall Street bull statue, arguing it only survives today because of the ordinary officials along the way, an art school dean, a policeman, a mayor, who quietly chose to let a bit of deviance through rather than shutting it down. Via Experimental History.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great one.

item.title: Byte-sized — Wednesday, 8 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, the eighth of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
The yen has fallen to its weakest level against the dollar since nineteen eighty six. It's down around three and a half percent against the dollar over six months, eleven percent over the past year, and roughly thirty five percent over three years, and on a broader trade weighted basis its value has halved over the past four decades. The Bank of Japan has spent close to seventy billion dollars this year alone trying to slow the slide, and is reportedly no longer telegraphing its interventions, instead springing them on currency speculators by surprise. Analysts blame a mix of short term pressures, including the wide gap between American and Japanese interest rates and higher oil prices forcing more yen sales to pay for energy imports, layered on top of longer running problems like Japan's shrinking workforce and heavy government debt. Prime Minister Takaichi has responded with a new stimulus package worth around two point three trillion dollars, aimed at technology and strategic industries, though critics warn the extra borrowing needed to fund it will only keep the yen under pressure. Via International Intrigue.
South Korea's memory chip makers are living through an extraordinary boom. One Samsung executive reportedly said this year's profit alone will exceed the company's entire cumulative semiconductor profit of the past forty years, with second quarter earnings expected to jump roughly eighteenfold on a year earlier. The driver is soaring demand for the memory chips that power AI data centres, a squeeze so severe that Apple was forced to raise Mac and iPad prices by up to a quarter last week, with memory prices industry wide up five to tenfold. In response, Samsung and SK Hynix have announced plans to invest around five hundred and twenty billion dollars over the next fifteen years to build a new domestic chip hub, though spread over that timeframe it's a more modest annual increase than the headline number suggests. Via Benedict Evans's newsletter and International Intrigue.
India's prime minister Narendra Modi is midway through an Indo-Pacific tour, having arrived in Jakarta on a trip that will also take him to Australia and New Zealand. Critical minerals and defence cooperation are high on the agenda, including talk of Indonesia buying India's BrahMos cruise missiles. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Anthropic says it's found something like an internal notepad inside Claude's mind. New research describes an internal region the company calls J space, which behaves like a workspace holding the concepts Claude is actively using while it reasons, distinct from the visible chain of thought text it shows users. Anthropic says the structure emerged on its own during training rather than being deliberately built in, and when researchers swapped one internal concept for another, say spider for ant, in a question about how many legs something has, Claude's answer changed to match. When they artificially removed this workspace, Claude could still chat normally and recall facts, but its ability to solve multi step problems collapsed, suggesting this is where its harder reasoning actually happens. Anthropic is careful to say this doesn't settle whether Claude is conscious or feels anything, a live and sometimes tetchy debate the company has had with Microsoft's AI head Mustafa Suleyman. Via The Rundown and TLDR.
Anthropic also keeps signing eye watering infrastructure deals. Data centre operator TeraWulf has agreed a twenty year lease with the company expected to bring in around nineteen billion dollars in revenue, covering a Kentucky campus with roughly four hundred megawatts of computing capacity. Anthropic has separately released a self hosted enterprise gateway for rolling out Claude Code through Amazon and Google's clouds, and is reportedly in talks with Samsung about designing its own AI chip. Via TLDR and Benedict Evans's newsletter.
Nvidia's next generation AI server system has slipped by more than a year. The Kyber rack scale architecture, designed to link one hundred and forty four of the company's upcoming Rubin Ultra chips into a single giant computer, won't now arrive until twenty twenty eight, after manufacturing problems with a key circuit board. It's a sign that Nvidia's breakneck annual release schedule is starting to bump up against the limits of what factories can actually build. Via TLDR.
Cheaper, smaller AI models are starting to squeeze the market. Tencent has fully open sourced its Hy3 model, which needs less than half the hardware of the rival GLM five point two, though GLM still wins on coding benchmarks. Analysts think the shift toward smaller, cheaper models could trigger what one report called an AI margin collapse, as everyday tasks get handled by inexpensive models rather than premium ones. Small models are also proving useful in healthcare and agriculture in places without heavy data centre infrastructure, and one study found a cheap model can discard over two thirds of unnecessary retrieved text while still keeping ninety six percent of what actually matters. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture.
European fintech had a mixed day. Banking software firm Thought Machine has crossed one hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue, with its chief executive eyeing a possible stock market listing in twenty twenty eight and wanting to double both revenue and customer numbers before then. Digital bank Starling is cutting around a hundred and thirty jobs as it leans further into automation, while buy now pay later firm Klarna won just under two billion dollars in an antitrust lawsuit against Google. Via Sifted.
The first European quantum computing company has floated on the Nasdaq. Finnish firm IQM listed via a merger with a shell company, with shares opening at around twelve dollars seventy, dipping, then recovering to close its first day near thirteen dollars and climbing further the day after. The float values IQM at around two point three billion dollars, a far lower multiple of revenue than the American quantum firm IonQ commands, though investors called the debut a solid one. Via Sifted.
A new survey suggests the tech workforce is splitting in two. Of nearly six thousand tech workers surveyed, whether someone feels amplified or diminished by AI turned out to be the single strongest predictor of how they feel about their career, ahead of seniority, role, or company size. Significant burnout jumped from forty five percent last year to fifty six percent this year, career optimism fell, and more than half of respondents said they wouldn't recommend a newcomer follow their own career path. Tellingly, fear of AI taking their job directly ranked low on the list of worries; people were far more concerned about being expected to do more for the same pay, or that the pace of work has simply become unsustainable. Via Lenny's Newsletter.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Congo is playing hardball over cobalt. After exporters missed a July the fifth deadline, Kinshasa is reassigning unused export quotas to a new state run entity, a move mining giants Glencore and CMOC blame on a government system glitch rather than any fault of their own. Congo supplies around seventy percent of the world's cobalt, a critical mineral for batteries, so the standoff matters well beyond central Africa. Via International Intrigue.
British officials had their logins stolen. Several UK government email accounts were compromised after attackers exploited so called FortiBleed vulnerabilities, with the stolen credentials reportedly being sold on the dark web for around sixty thousand dollars. Researchers say the intrusion doesn't look state sponsored, but the attackers appear to be Russian speakers. Via TLDR.
Canada has chosen its next submarine builder, and it isn't South Korea. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Germany's TKMS, working on a joint German Norwegian Arctic capable design, will build Canada's fleet of around twelve new conventionally powered submarines, beating out South Korea's Hanwha, with deliveries expected in the twenty thirties. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Here's an idea worth stealing if you work in marketing: stop worrying about clicks, start worrying about being named. Growth consultant Kevin Indig has spent the past year studying how people actually use AI search tools, and found that almost nobody clicks through on citations, even when a brand is the hidden source behind an answer. What matters far more is whether the AI actually says a brand's name out loud, since his research found only around one in eight brands that get quoted from also get mentioned by name. His advice for getting mentioned is to write like a wire reporter rather than a novelist, putting the most important facts right at the start, because AI systems weight the introduction heavily and barely read the middle. Via Amanda Natividad's newsletter.
And one for community builders: stop recruiting speakers, grow them instead. Skift's Women Leading Travel network fills its event stages almost entirely from members who are already active in the community between events, through smaller meetups, virtual workshops, and spotlight features, rather than through a cold outside application process. This autumn it's running leadership events on that model in New York, Montreal, Chicago, Las Vegas, and London. Via Skift.
Now, over to one interesting thing to leave you with.
A newsletter called Why Is This Interesting points out that America's measles cases, which averaged just four a week for three decades, have jumped to fifty eight a week since the start of last year, and argues it's a visible symptom of a much bigger problem: American scientists quietly leaving the country. Job applications abroad from American scientists rose by around a third last year, dozens of senior researchers have relocated to China, and the European Union has launched a five hundred million euro fund specifically designed to attract them to Europe. The piece's point is that research funding, like a vaccine programme, has knock on effects that take years to show up, and by the time the damage is visible, in outbreaks or in the technologies that never got invented, it's already too late to easily undo.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great one.

item.title: Byte-sized — Tuesday, 7 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, the seventh of July, and here are seven stories to catch you up.
Chinese AI models are closing the gap with the West. A new analysis argues that last year's DeepSeek moment was not a one off event but the start of a pattern. The newest model from the Chinese lab Zed dot AI, called G L M five point two, now performs close to the leading American closed models on coding and agent tasks, echoing the shock that DeepSeek's earlier release caused within the American AI community. Analysts say this steady catching up has real consequences for the cost of building frontier AI, for the spread of open weight models that anyone can download and modify, and for how Washington sets AI policy going forward. Via CSIS.
Meta says its next model is already rivalling the best from OpenAI. Meta's superintelligence chief, Alexandr Wang, reportedly told staff that a model in training, nicknamed Watermelon, has matched the performance of G P T five point five, while using around ten times the computing power of its predecessor, which only launched in April. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg separately said progress on AI agents across the whole industry has been slower than expected, though Wang pushed back, saying that was a comment on the industry generally rather than Meta specifically, and promised an update to Meta's existing model with strong coding and agent improvements soon, alongside a coding model to rival Anthropic's best. Via The Rundown.
Washington is moving fast on AI and quantum policy. President Trump has signed an executive order titled Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security, which asks AI companies to voluntarily submit powerful new models for government benchmarking of their cyber capabilities before wider release, with early access going to selected trusted partners chosen with government input. Two further executive orders aim to accelerate American quantum computing research and push federal agencies toward encryption that can resist future quantum based attacks by the end of the decade. Separately, the Federal Communications Commission has expanded a ban on importing telecoms and surveillance equipment from several Chinese manufacturers, citing national security risks, with the wider restrictions due to take effect early this month. Via CSIS.
Twenty twenty six is shaping up as the year of the AI lab. A wave of star researchers are leaving the likes of Meta and Google DeepMind to start their own ventures, and investors are pouring in billions to back them. In Paris, three former Meta and OpenAI staff are seeking four hundred million dollars for a startup called Aire, aiming to build an AI system that can automate scientific research from end to end. Yann LeCun's new venture, AMI Labs, has already raised over a billion dollars in seed funding, while two London based labs, Recursive Superintelligence and Ineffable Intelligence, raised five hundred million and one point one billion dollars respectively in April alone. Via Sifted.
Europe's fintech giants are still in no hurry to go public. Banking software firm Thought Machine says twenty twenty eight now looks like the likely year for its stock market debut, echoing a similar delay announced by Revolut earlier this year, with its chief executive citing a lack of investor appetite for risk after a run of disappointing European listings. Meanwhile, digital bank Starling is cutting around a hundred and thirty jobs as it leans further into automation, and voice AI company ElevenLabs is reportedly in talks for a fresh share sale that would value the business at twenty two billion dollars. Via Sifted.
New figures underline both the toll of the war in Ukraine and the fragility of global trade routes. Combined Russian and Ukrainian casualties have now passed two million, with Russian losses running at close to eight times Ukrainian losses so far this year, a sharp rise from a ratio closer to two or three to one earlier in the conflict. Elsewhere, the Malacca Strait now carries a larger share of the world's seaborne oil trade than the Strait of Hormuz, and more than thirteen million American jobs depend on trade with Canada and Mexico, a reminder of how much economic weight rides on those relationships as trade tensions continue. Via CSIS.
Finally, cyber and undersea tensions are rising too. Israel's cyber chief says Iranian cyberattacks have roughly tripled over the past year, climbing from around sixteen hundred incidents to nearly five thousand, following the recent American and Israeli military operations against Iran. And in the North Atlantic, Britain's defence secretary John Healey has revealed that UK forces tracked Russian attack and spy submarines detected close to the undersea cables that carry much of the world's data and communications, underlining growing concern about threats to that infrastructure. Via CSIS.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great one.
